title: One whole workflow
caption: Follow the summer-party workflow from goal to plan. These are illustrative oversight choices, not defaults; use the level that fits each task.
goal: Goal: bring 200 people from five offices together next summer, within €60,000
workflowLabel: The summer-party workflow, stage by stage

planRequirements.delivers: four work areas, Venue and date first

requirementsResearch.receives: the chosen Venue and date work area
requirementsResearch.checkedBy: the organiser signs off this set

researchPage.delivers: sourced venue, travel and date findings
researchPage.checkedBy: sources support claims; gaps stay open

twoLevels: You design the stages; the agent steers inside each task

steps.process: Pick one recurring process. Mark each step: agent or person, in, on or out of the loop. “Out” means no intervention during that task.
steps.contract: Write the handoff clearly. What the task receives and delivers, and how its result can be checked; checks need not all be human.
steps.conway: Use Conway’s law as a prompt. If team boundaries make handoffs work against the goal, consider another design.
steps.skills: Develop useful capabilities. Breaking work down, writing clear handoffs and checking results.

workflow-and-agent-two-levels.description: Anthropic separates workflows, orchestrated through predefined code paths, from agents that direct their own process; reading the quiz example as a path you design with steps the agent steers is an application of that split, not a claim the source makes [1].

one-whole-workflow.title: One whole workflow
one-whole-workflow.script: Let's bring the Episode together with the actual summer-party Workflow. Its goal is to bring 200 people from five offices together next summer, within €60,000. It moves through Plan, Requirements, Research and Page to a one-page party plan. The oversight choices shown are examples, not defaults.

in-on-or-out-per-step.title: In, on or out per step
in-on-or-out-per-step.script: The labels are illustrative choices for this Workflow: Plan and Research are on the loop; Requirements and Page are in the loop. People choose a suitable level for each task, considering its risks, checks and context. Out means no intervention during that task, not necessarily no later review.

a-contract-at-every-handoff.title: A contract at every handoff
a-contract-at-every-handoff.script: The cards make three handoffs visible: what the next stage receives, what it should deliver and how the result can be checked. Here, the organiser signs off the research questions; sources support the findings, and gaps stay open. Checks can be automated or human where appropriate.

designed-around-the-goal.title: Designed around the goal
designed-around-the-goal.script: Notice that this example starts from the party goal, not from the org chart. Use Conway's law as a prompt to examine whether team boundaries help or hinder the goal; it is not a diagnosis by itself. Breaking work down, writing clear handoffs and checking results are useful capabilities to consider, not a universal checklist. Start with one process and decide what fits its tasks.
